title: In 1835 a New York paper told readers that astronomers had seen bat-people on the Moon

cover.alt: On a fantastical Moon with lilac crystal spires and a blue Earth in a starry sky, a copper-haired man-bat spreads its wings beside a small blue unicorn.

body: In August 1835 the New York *Sun*, a penny paper, ran six articles claiming that **Sir John Herschel**, observing at the Cape of Good Hope, had used an enormous new telescope to see life on the Moon. They were said to come from a supplement to the *Edinburgh Journal of Science*, which had printed no such thing. Readers met bison with a hairy veil over their eyes, blue one-horned goats, beavers that walked on two legs and used fire, and winged, copper-haired 'man-bats'. Many believed it: Edgar Allan Poe later wrote that 'not one person in ten discredited it'. The *Sun* never owned up. A rival paper named the reporter **Richard Adams Locke** as the author, and in 1840 he admitted it, calling it satire. Herschel, who had nothing to do with it, complained of being pestered about it from all quarters, in four languages.

slides.alt: A New York street of brick houses. A newsboy in a cap waves a newspaper with a picture of a winged creature, shouting; a man in a top hat and a woman in a bonnet stop to look.
slides.caption: New York, 25 August 1835. The Sun has astonishing news from the Moon, by way of a Scottish science journal.

bubbles.text: Great astronomical discoveries! Life on the Moon! One cent!
bubbles.speaker: A newsboy

slides.alt: Under a starry sky, a colossal telescope with a gleaming lens, held up on timber struts, points at the Moon. A tiny man in a frock coat stands beside it.
slides.caption: The story's telescope has a lens 24 feet across, weighs nearly seven tons and magnifies 42,000 times.

slides.alt: A fantastical Moon: square-topped lilac crystal spires, green valleys, a lake and the blue Earth in a black sky. In front stand brown, shaggy bison with a curtain of hair over their eyes.
slides.caption: Through the lens: lilac crystal spires, and bison with a hairy veil over the eyes, lifted and lowered by their ears.

slides.alt: On the same lunar meadow, a goat-sized bluish creature with a beard and a single long horn, and a smaller one by the lake.
slides.caption: Next, a goat-sized creature of a bluish lead colour, with a beard and a single horn.

slides.alt: A brown beaver walks upright on its hind legs, carrying its baby in its arms. Behind it a hut glows with firelight, smoke curling from it.
slides.caption: Then beavers that walk on two legs, carry their young in their arms and live in huts with fires.

slides.alt: Two copper-haired creatures with human faces and folded bat wings stand on the Moon chatting, while two more fly overhead.
slides.caption: 28 August: the man-bats. About four feet tall, covered in short copper-coloured hair, and winged.

bubbles.text: Do you get the feeling we're being watched?
bubbles.speaker: A man-bat

slides.alt: Back on the New York street, a man in a top hat clutches the paper in shock, a woman in a bonnet gasps and a newsboy grins.
slides.caption: New York laps it up. Poe later reckoned that 'not one person in ten' doubted it. The Sun claims a world-record sale.

slides.alt: A sunny hillside at the Cape, a flat-topped mountain behind and a real telescope on a wooden stand. Sir John Herschel, sweating and grim, holds the newspaper over a heap of letters.
slides.caption: At the Cape, the real Sir John Herschel knows nothing of it, until the letters start arriving.

bubbles.text: I have been pestered from all quarters with that ridiculous hoax. In English, French, Italian and German!
bubbles.speaker: Sir John Herschel

slides.question: Why couldn't New Yorkers easily check the story in 1835?
options: Herschel was far away in South Africa
The Moon was hidden that month
The Sun was printed in Edinburgh
slides.explanation: Herschel was observing at the Cape of Good Hope, and news took weeks to cross the oceans. The Edinburgh journal it cited had printed no such thing.

source.label: Museum of Hoaxes: The Great Moon Hoax
